division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.45   A third party claim must
(a) be in Form 16,
(b) comply with the rules about pleadings in Part 13, Division
3,
(c) be filed and served on the plaintiff and the third party
defendant, whether or not the third party defendant is
already a party to the action,
(i) within 6 months after the date on which the
defendant filed a statement of defence or demand for
notice, and
(ii) before judgment is entered against the defendant or
the defendant is noted in default,
and
(d) be accompanied, when it is served on the third party
defendant, with a copy of the statement of claim served on
the defendant.

commentary.text: Rule 3.45 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.45. 1. Extension of Time Rule 66 does not provide any guidance as to when the court should or should not extend the time allowed for filing and serving third-party proceedings. I concur with the statement of the Master in Kreway v. Renfrew Chrysler Plymouth et al. and Chrysler Canada Ltd., [1973] 1 W.W.R. 461, where he states that reasons for refusing to extend time are: (1) inordinate delay; (2) absence of credible excuse; and (3) prejudice This decision was subsequently approved by the Alberta Supreme Court, [1973] 1 W.W.R. 462. Edmonton & Rural Auxilliary Hospital & Nursing Home District No. 24 v. Bittorf-Holland-Christianson Architects Ltd. (1981), 33 A.R. 60 at 63 (Q.B.). In a later decision, the Alberta Court of Appeal considered delay as: … a reason for refusing a third party notice where the defendant is alerted by the pleading as to the nature of the claim and the magnitude of the claim against him when he makes his election not to issue a third party notice. That election is made when the time established by the rules expires. E.S.M. Transport Ltd. v. Western Mack Truck (Edmonton) Ltd. (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 115 at 117 (C.A.). As to when to bring the application: … an order extending time for filing and serving a third party notice should not be made unless there is material filed to support such order. Sheahan v. Fischer (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 300 at 302 (Master). In Lister v. Calgary (City) (1997), 47 Alta. L.R. (3d) 14, the Court of Appeal commented on the need for evidence in support of an application to extend time for filing. At pp. 16-17, the court said: Where a party seeks a significant time extension, it is expected to give evidence to explain the delay, i.e. why prompt compliance did not occur. Maybe it would be different if the extension sought was slight, but here the delay was over four and one-half years. Evidence must be proper admissible evidence such as an affidavit, not mere allegations by counsel. The cases on time extensions generally, and those on later third party notices, seem to agree on those points. . . . . . … the onus of proof is on the City, which is the one which moved for leave to issue a pleading four and one-half years late. The third party is not obliged to lead any evidence at all, let alone evidence which excludes doubt. The onus is on the City to lead evidence which justifies the late pleading by explaining the delay. In Kaptian v. Hardy (1999), 251 A.R. 291 (Q.B.), at p. 295, Chief Justice Moore said: The length of any delay is relevant as it relates to: the reasonableness of an excuse for the delay, prejudice because of the delay, third party procedure benefits. The test can therefore be subsumed into two parts. 1. Reasonable Excuse A defendant has the burden of proof on an application to extend the time limit of rule 66(4). The six month time frame open to a defendant to file a third party notice gives the defendant an opportunity to consider potential third parties. Any delay after the expiry of the six months requires a reasonable excuse. If a defendant has no reasonable excuse for the delay then leave to add a third party will be denied. 2. Prejudice If a defendant has a reasonable excuse for the delay, then the court must balance the potential prejudice to the third party and the plaintiff because of the delay against the benefits of adding the third party. If the prejudice outweighs the benefits of third party procedure, then leave to add a third party will be denied. However, in Flight v. Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211, 2001 CarswellAlta 322, 284 A.R. 117, Madam Justice Moreau disagreed with Chief Justice Moore's requirement that any delay beyond the six-month period requires a reasonable excuse. At p. 126, Her Ladyship said: … I am of the view that the proper test for an application to strike a third party notice is as suggested by the authorities which preceded Kaptian, supra and that prejudice is still a factor to be weighed along with the nature of the delay and whether it can be reasonably excused, unless the delay is significant. In that event, the absence of a reasonable excuse for the delay effectively overpowers any need on the part of the third party to demonstrate actual prejudice. I therefore respectfully disagree with my former colleague that every case of delay beyond the six-month time frame contemplated by rule 66(4) requires the defendant to advance a reasonable excuse before any consideration of prejudice comes into play. I would agree with the approach taken in [Grandwood Flooring Western Ltd. v. Prism Construction Co. and Edson (1986), 43 Alta. L.R. (2d) 337 (Master)], namely that a short delay would result in a different weighing exercise, focusing primarily on the existence of any prejudice. As one moves further away from the six-month deadline, the weighing exercise will focus more on whether the delay is excusable. In the case of a significant delay … failure to advance a reasonable excuse for the delay will, without more, be fatal to an application to extend time. In Dean v. Kociniak, 2001 ABQB 412, 2001 CarswellAlta 709, 289 A.R. 201, 92 Alta. L.R. (3d) 92, Slatter J. said, at p. 223: With respect, I agree with the decision in Flight v. Dillon that the sequential test set out in Kaptian v. Hardy is not inflexible. The length of the delay, the explanation for the delay, and the relative prejudice to the two parties are to be considered concurrently when the Court exercises its discretion to allow or reject a late Third Party claim. Obviously, the longer the delay, the more the Court might assume prejudice from the mere passage of time, as memories will tend to weaken, the litigation will tend to advance further, and the Third Party might increasingly be prejudiced by the passage of time. However, the mere fact that there is no satisfactory explanation for some or all of the delay is not fatal to the application. In Builders Holdings Ltd. v. Gasland Properties Ltd., 2001 ABQB 823, 2001 CarswellAlta 1740, 306 A.R. 163, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231, Mr. Justice Lee said, at p. 246: In my opinion, with the exception of Kaptian, the trend of the case law has been to consider all three factors, balancing the length of the delay with the requirement of an explanation and with the absence of prejudice. The longer the delay, the greater the requirement for a reasonable explanation. Prejudice will always be an important factor. In Kwik-Kopy Printing Canada Corp. v. Skoreik (2002), 324 A.R. 126 (Q.B.), at p. 135, Watson J. held that “it is within the jurisdiction of a Court to look at whether there is an air of reality to the foundation of the Third Party Notice in deciding whether to grant leave to file such outside of the time limit.” In Hein v. Barrett (2008), 96 Alta. L.R. (4th) 397 (Master), Master Hanebury summarized the law (at pp. 403-404): 23 From this case law the following principles emerge: 1. Three factors are considered when determining an application to extend the time for filing a third party notice: the length of the delay, the reason for the delay and the prejudice to the third party. 2. Depending on the length of the delay, different weights may be given to the other two factors. 3. For a short period of delay, the primary consideration is prejudice, and an excuse for the delay is of less importance. 4. The relevant importance of these factors is reversed as the length of the delay increases. The longer the delay the greater the importance of an excuse for the delay and the lesser the importance of the question of prejudice. 5. When there is a significant delay, the lack of a reasonable excuse, without more, will be fatal to the application. 6. The pace of the litigation can also be considered when deciding the weight to be assigned to each of the three factors. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R. 72, 79 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes said, at paragraphs 497–500: 497 Rule 3.45 requires a third party claim to be filed and served within six months of the filing of the statement of defence. This time may be extended after the consideration of the following three factors: (1) the length of delay; (2) the reason for the delay; and (3) the prejudice to the third party: Alliance Pipeline at para 10 citing Flight v. Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211, 284 AR 117 [Flight]; Dean; and Builders Holdings Ltd. v. Gasland Properties, Ltd, 2001 ABCA 823, 306 AR 163. 498 The requirement to explain the delay is mandatory: Mangat v. Allen, 2010 ABQB 264 at para 10. 499 When the delay is relatively short, more weight is given to the existence of prejudice resulting from the delay and less to the length of delay. As the length of the delay becomes longer, more weight is given to the reason for the delay and less to the existence of prejudice: Spartek Systems Inc v. Brown, 2009 ABQB 705 at para 14, 481 AR 213 [Spartek]; Flight; Dean; Alliance Pipeline at para 10. A delay of approximately 10–14 months is considered relatively short: Alliance Pipeline at para 11. When the delay is longer, the defendant seeking the extension must give evidence explaining the delay. Evidence explaining the delay was required in Lister v. Calgary (City) (1997), 193 AR 218 (CA) where the delay was 4.5 years: para 20. Leave will be denied if the delay is long and no evidence is provided to explain it. In Hein v. Barrett, 2008 ABQB 548, leave was refused where an insufficient explanation was given for a seven-year delay. The pace of the litigation is another factor to be considered in weighing the three factors: Spartek at para 14. 500 The viability of the proposed third party claim will be considered when determining whether an extension of time to file the third party claim should be granted. The claim must have an “air of reality”: LaBell v. Jo (R) (1990), 105 AR 319 at para. 4. In Nelson & Nelson v. Condominium Corporation No. 0013187, 2019 ABQB 426, 2019 CarswellAlta 1148, 93 C.C.L.I. (5th) 344, Justice Hollins said: [49] The 6-month time period in Rule 3.45 can be extended in the discretion of the Court; Rule 13.5. In the absence of an agreement to extend that time, a defendant can apply for an extension of time to add a third party. However, that defendant must show that the delay in applying to add the third party has not been inordinate, that there is a credible excuse for the delay and that the late addition of a third party will not cause prejudice; Condominium Plan 9812082 v Battistella Developments Inc, 2014 ABQB 644 (CanLII) at para.15. … [51] As (now Chief) Justice Moreau explained in Flight v Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211 (CanLII) at para.29, where the delay is short, the focus will be less on the excuse offered for the delay than on the potential prejudice. Where the delay is longer, the prejudice may be assumed and the excuse for the delay becomes more important. Where there has been significant delay, a reasonable excuse must be provided.

BOOK_C.title: Form of third party claim
BOOK_C.operative_text_raw:
A third party claim must (a) be in Form 16, (b) comply with the rules about pleadings in Part 13 [Technical Rules], Division 3 , [Pleadings]
(c) be filed and served on the plaintiff and the third party defendant, whether or not the third party defendant is already a party to the action, (i) within 6 months after the date on which the defendant filed a statement of defence or demand for notice, and (ii) before judgment is entered against the defendant or the defendant is noted in default, and (d) be accompanied, when it is served on the third party defendant, with a copy of the statement of claim served on the defendant.

commentary.text:
This rule sets out the form required and the fact that third party claims must comply with the rules about pleadings in Part 13, Division 3. A third party claim is to be drafted as any other pleading, including setting out the facts necessary to establish a valid claim.
Time Limitation to File – There is a time limitation to file and serve a third party claim, being six months after the date on which the defendant (the party issuing the third party claim) filed a statement of defence or a demand for notice and before judgment is entered against the defendant or the defendant is noted in default. The case law informs the application of this six-month limitation.
Extension of Deadline – Key factors in considering whether to grant an extension are whether there has been inordinate delay, no credible or reasonable excuse and prejudice. H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., [2024] A.J. No. 903, 2024 ABKB 428 at paras. 20-21 (Alta. K.B.); Condominium Plan 9812082 v. Battistella Developments Inc.,[2014] A.J. No. 1167, 2014 ABQB 644 at para. 15 (Alta. Q.B.).
An additional factor may be whether the proposed third party claim has merit, which involves a low threshold sometimes described as “air of reality”. H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., [2024] A.J. No. 903, 2024 ABKB 428 at paras. 23-24 (Alta. K.B.); , Condominium Corp. No. 9813678 v. Statesman Corp.
Where the delay in advancing a third party claim is short, the primary focus of the application is on the excuse offered and the prejudice suffered. The requirement to explain the delay [2008] A.J. No. 904, 2008 ABQB 495 at para. 46 (Alta. Q.B.).
